chunks: Balance charging and when it is needed. The question: What is balance charging? When is it needed?
Balance charging means charging a multi-cell pack so that every cell ends at the same voltage, not just so the total looks right.
In a series pack, the same current flows through every cell, but the cells are not identical. One cell reaches 4. 2 volts first.
A charger that only watches the total keeps pushing, and that cell goes over its limit.
Think of four friends splitting a restaurant bill. The total on the receipt can be exactly right while one person quietly paid far too much and another far too little.
Checking only the total hides the problem. Balance charging is looking at what each person paid, and adjusting until each share is fair.
For a battery, an unfair share means a cell pushed past its safe voltage.
The charger only sees the sum: 4. 35 + 4. 20 + 4. 15 + 4. 10 = 16. 80 volts, a perfect 4S full-charge value.
Cell 1 is already 150 millivolts over its limit while cell 4 is still short of full.
Series pack: cells connected end to end, so their voltages add ("LiPo cell voltage range and why").
Balance lead: an extra connector with a wire to each cell junction, so the charger can read every cell.
Passive balancing: bleeding extra charge from the fullest cells through a resistor ("Cell balancing: why, when, what if missing").
Active balancing: moving charge from fuller cells to emptier ones. Cell spread: the voltage difference between the highest and lowest cell.
Take a 4S pack charged to 16. 80 volts, which is 4 times 4. 20 volts. The total can be right even when the cells are uneven: 4. 35 plus 4. 20 plus 4. 15 plus 4. 10 equals 16.
80 volts. The first cell is 150 millivolts over its 4. 20 volts limit, although the pack voltage looks perfect. With a balance lead, the charger sees that cell and bleeds it.
A 47 ohms bleed resistor at 4. 2 volts draws about 89 milliamps, so removing a 110 milliamp hours excess (5% of a 2200 milliamp hours cell) takes about 1. 2 hours.
That is the whole idea.
"Balance charging makes every cell in a series pack finish at the same voltage, not just the pack total.
Series cells get the same current but differ in capacity and starting charge, so one hits 4. 2 volts first.
The charger uses a tap on each cell to see that, then bleeds the full cell through a resistor, or moves charge to weaker cells, while the rest catch up.
You need it for any pack of two or more series cells, especially mismatched or aged ones."
